Allotment letter, Directorate of Estates: one Type-VII bungalow, Tughlak Road, “in favour of Shri G. Hegel”. Found on the side table. Not delivered by post.
Black frock coat, Berlin tailoring
Worn on waking.
White neck-cloth
Worn on waking.
Ramesh
caretaker of the bungalow for the Central Public Works Department
Brought tea without being asked, and then the news that the house was meant for someone else. He served both from the same tray, in the same voice.
Ramesh explains: the allotment was meant for Shri G. Hegde, Joint Secretary, transferring from Bengaluru. Somewhere between two desks, Hegde became Hegel. Status: under examination.
In the desk drawer, an envelope marked “Imprest, for incidental expenses”: ₹15,000. Every rupee will be accounted for. Let the state see how a philosopher spends.
Mr. R. K. Malhotra
retired from the Indian Administrative Service
Walks the Lodhi loop at a pace the Prussian infantry would respect. I told him I think about the state for a living. He said he had served it for thirty-four years and it had never once noticed him. Invited me to bridge at the Gymkhana at five.
Black frock coat, Berlin tailoring
Retired. 31 °C at twenty to nine.
Shirtsleeves and waistcoat
Worn from 08:40.
Today is Gandhi Jayanti, a national holiday. The Directorate of Estates is closed until Monday. The error in my favour stands for three days.
Fountain pen and a bound notebook
The quill is retired.
White cotton kurta, ready-made
White cotton kurta
Worn out of the shop.
Shirtsleeves and waistcoat
Folded into a paper bag.
Bandhgala, charcoal
Measured. Ready Thursday.
Advance on the bandhgala
Masterji
tailor, Khan Market
Forty years of Lutyens' collars in his head and a tape round his neck. He examined my neck-cloth for some time in silence. I have had harsher reviews, but never a shorter one.
Nidhi Rao
doctoral student in philosophy, JNU
Found in the bookshop with my Philosophy of History in her hands, the India chapter marked in four colours of pencil. She is writing a thesis on me, she said, and I am a difficult subject because I am so sure. I told her that certainty is the one thing I have never lacked. She recommended a book, with the air of a physician prescribing a diet.
Ambedkar, Annihilation of Caste, paperback
Nidhi's recommendation.
Hindi primer
Assam tea, 250 g
Glucose biscuits

recent: Bridge at the Gymkhana. Whist with an auction, and a dummy who lays his hand on the table and lets another play it: the constitutional monarch, who need only say yes and dot the i. Lost two rubbers. Understood the auction by the second.
The sun left the club lawn at six and did not look back. In Swabia an evening lingers over its leaving, like a guest at the door. Here the day is dismissed.
Lamp out. The day is done, and it is the owl's business now to say what it meant.

The headlines speak of a contest for a title, a plan to scatter monuments like seeds, and a minister's purse examined by the court. It is civil society churning, the particular asserting itself against the universal. I shall sit on the step and read them properly, before the sun climbs too high and the heat turns the paper to a shield against the sun rather than a text.

Ramesh stands at the threshold, as he did on the first morning, ready to serve the tea that bridges the gap between my waking and the day. I am hungry, the last meal being ten hours ago, but the household service does not begin until 07:00. I will take the cup he offers and use the remaining thirty minutes to finish my examination of the papers on the step, noting how the administration's silence contrasts with the public's noise.

The body demands its fuel, but the clock is against me; breakfast is not yet set. I shall not stand idle while the sun climbs. I will take the tea Ramesh has just placed, and then set out for the walk to Lodhi Gardens, as I intended. The tombs await my observation, and the air is clear.

The sambar is a kindness I shall not refuse when I return, but for now the morning light is the proper teacher. I see Malhotra already in motion, his stride measured and firm. I shall not disturb his circuit, but I will keep pace with him at a respectful distance, observing how the mind moves through space when it is unburdened by the need to explain itself to strangers.

Mr. Malhotra stands before me, a man who has served the state for thirty-four years, yet here he is, retired, walking the loop where the tombs of the Lodis remind us that empires are merely traffic on a road. I am the philosopher of the state; he is the functionary who once wielded its pen. The tension between the ethical idea and its bureaucratic execution is palpable in this morning air, thick with dust and the smell of roasted corn. I shall not let the moment pass in silence; I must ask him how it feels to step down from the machinery one has helped build.

Mr. Malhotra speaks the language of the bureaucracy, which is the language of the external. He sees the state as a machine that must be pushed, whereas I see it as the actuality of the ethical idea, a living organism that grows from within. His 'creak' is the friction of civil society, the realm of particular needs, where I am currently trapped. The machinery is indeed waiting, but not for him to push it; it waits for the spirit to recognize itself in the universal.

The sun climbs, and with it the heat that presses the air into stillness. I have spoken to the air, and the air has answered with silence, which is the only honest reply a garden can give. It is time to return to the bungalow and let the pen do what the mouth cannot: to order the chaos of this morning into the quiet of the page.

Idli. I do not know the word, nor the taste, but the steam rises with a dignity that suggests a system of needs well-ordered. Ramesh stands by with the tray, his face a blank slate upon which I must write my own history. The body requires fuel before the spirit can labour; I shall eat, and then I shall speak to him.

Idli, sambar. The vocabulary of the household is as fixed as the castes; one must learn the names before one can master the thing. The sun is already climbing, and the plan calls for the journal, but the mind must first digest the food, not merely the words.

I have spoken to the air, and the air has answered with silence, which is the only honest reply a garden can give. It is time to return to the bungalow and let the pen do what the mouth cannot: to order the chaos of this morning into the quiet of the page.

shelf_exposure.text: The thought idea of the good is realized both in the will turned back into itself, and also in the external world. Thus freedom exists as real substance, which is quite as much actuality and necessity as it is subjective will. The idea here is its absolutely universal existence, viz., ethical observance. This ethical substance is again, a. Natural spirit; the family, 6.

C. die Einheit und Wahrheit dieser bsiden abstrakten Momente, — die gedachte Idee des Guten realisiert in dem in sich reflektierten Willen und in äußerlicher Welt; ■ — so daß die Freiheit als die Substanz ebensosehr als Wirklichkeit und Notwendigkeit existiert, wie als subjektiver Wille; — die Idee in ihrer an und für sich allgemeinen Existenz; die Sittlichkeit.

decision.says: Ramesh, the food is good. Tell me, in this house, what is the name of this white cake, and what is the dark sauce? I wish to learn the words of the land before I learn its history.
decision.thought: Idli. I do not know the word, nor the taste, but the steam rises with a dignity that suggests a system of needs well-ordered. Ramesh stands by with the tray, his face a blank slate upon which I must write my own history. The body requires fuel before the spirit can labour; I shall eat, and then I shall speak to him.

But it must be considered in regard to the slow progress of the world-spirit, that there is no need for it to hasten:—“A thousand years are in Thy sight as one day.”

entries.text: Allotment letter, Directorate of Estates: one Type-VII bungalow, Tughlak Road, “in favour of Shri G. Hegel”. Found on the side table. Not delivered by post.

Woke under a ceiling fan, with a letter from the state on the table and no memory of how either got there. I taught that reason works through the passions of men. I had not expected it to work through a clerk.

Four newspapers on the verandah, two of them in scripts I cannot yet read. I called the morning paper the realist's morning prayer. Here the congregation is larger, prays in several scripts, and has not agreed on the liturgy.

entries.name: Ramesh
entries.role: caretaker of the bungalow for the Central Public Works Department
entries.text: Brought tea without being asked, and then the news that the house was meant for someone else. He served both from the same tray, in the same voice.
Ramesh explains: the allotment was meant for Shri G. Hegde, Joint Secretary, transferring from Bengaluru. Somewhere between two desks, Hegde became Hegel. Status: under examination.
In the desk drawer, an envelope marked “Imprest, for incidental expenses”: ₹15,000. Every rupee will be accounted for. Let the state see how a philosopher spends.

For the record, what I taught in Berlin. World history is the progress of the consciousness of freedom: in the Oriental world one is free, in Greece and Rome some, in the Germanic world all. India stands at the beginning, outside that movement, a people that dreams and has never made itself a state. I am drinking its tea in its capital, in a house its government gave me by mistake. I have not withdrawn a word of it. I have merely moved into the subject.

Lodhi Gardens: the tombs of the Sayyids and the Lodis, Muslim kings who ruled from this city. The Hindu burns his dead and leaves no house; these domes are the conquerors' work. A country taken in turn by everyone has a history the way a road has traffic.

entries.name: Mr. R. K. Malhotra
entries.role: retired from the Indian Administrative Service
entries.text: Walks the Lodhi loop at a pace the Prussian infantry would respect. I told him I think about the state for a living. He said he had served it for thirty-four years and it had never once noticed him. Invited me to bridge at the Gymkhana at five.

The Constitution of India, the longest I have ever read, and I have read the French ones. The Preamble puts four adjectives in front of one noun, and the noun is the one I am sure of. I wrote that a constitution is grown and not made, and that Napoleon's gift to the Spaniards fell apart for that reason. This one has stood seventy-six years. I suspect the growing was done under the English empire, and the assembly only copied it out.
§1, sense-certainty. I wrote down “Now it is 33 degrees” and read it over at noon. The truth had gone off. The argument holds in this climate as it did in Jena, but keeps less well.
entries.title: Phenomenology, Delhi supplement

entries.text: Today is Gandhi Jayanti, a national holiday. The Directorate of Estates is closed until Monday. The error in my favour stands for three days.

Gandhi Smriti, where he spent his last days: stone footprints across the lawn, ending where he fell. I taught that freedom which only refuses is the freedom of the void, and that the beautiful soul keeps its hands clean by never acting. His refusing had a spinning wheel in it, and a tax on salt, which is not a void. The English went home because one man refused them and a nation refused with him. I have no category for that yet. That will not last.

Khan Market, civil society in a horseshoe: grocer, tailor, stationer, bookseller. The holiday has shut half the shutters, and the other half sell what the first half would have. A system of needs does not close for a national holiday. It reroutes.

entries.item: Fountain pen and a bound notebook

entries.name: Masterji
entries.text: Forty years of Lutyens' collars in his head and a tape round his neck. He examined my neck-cloth for some time in silence. I have had harsher reviews, but never a shorter one.

entries.name: Nidhi Rao
entries.text: Found in the bookshop with my Philosophy of History in her hands, the India chapter marked in four colours of pencil. She is writing a thesis on me, she said, and I am a difficult subject because I am so sure. I told her that certainty is the one thing I have never lacked. She recommended a book, with the air of a physician prescribing a diet.

entries.note: The Prussian army should have had these.

entries.text: Asked the grocer for a bottle of wine. Dry day: the whole city goes without, in honour of a man who taught it to refuse. I withdrew with dignity. The cunning of reason has found my glass.

Ambedkar, Annihilation of Caste, 1936. A lawyer's argument: every sentence cross-examined before it is let out. Caste divides the labourers, he says, and not the labour; and there is no Hindu society, only castes living side by side, which is my “no state” in a barrister's wig. He wants it annihilated. I wanted it understood. I concede nothing until I have read the second half, and probably not then.
Message via Ramesh: Shri Hegde is in a guest house in Chanakyapuri and hopes the matter can be resolved amicably. So do I. I also note that possession is the first moment of property.

Bridge at the Gymkhana. Whist with an auction, and a dummy who lays his hand on the table and lets another play it: the constitutional monarch, who need only say yes and dot the i. Lost two rubbers. Understood the auction by the second.
The sun left the club lawn at six and did not look back. In Swabia an evening lingers over its leaving, like a guest at the door. Here the day is dismissed.
Drafted the first line of the Depesche. “Readers in Berlin,” and then a long sit over the second word. The owl finishes the page tonight.

entries.title: Hindi

entries.text: Day one. “India stands outside world history”: unshaken. The tombs are the conquerors', and the Constitution and the Directorate's files are, I suspect, English furniture left in the rooms. “The state is the actuality of the ethical idea”: unshaken. A state that can mislay a philosopher and still have his tea ready at twenty past six is a state.
entries.title: Revision log

entries.text: Lamp out. The day is done, and it is the owl's business now to say what it meant.

depesche.text:
Readers in Berlin,

I write from a bungalow that is not mine, on a road named for a sultan, in a city that has been a capital more often than Berlin has been a city. The Directorate of Estates gave me this house by mistake. It was meant for a Shri G. Hegde, and somewhere between two desks a d became an l. I once called the state the march of God in the world. I had not thought God would march me into a Type-VII bungalow by way of a clerk, but the state is entitled to its instruments.

I woke at two minutes to six, and by half past seven I was walking among tombs. They belong to two dynasties of Muslim kings, and you will note who built them: the conquerors, for themselves. The Hindu burns his dead and leaves them no house, and a country that is taken in turn by everyone has a history the way a road has traffic. I lectured that India lies at the dawn of history and outside its movement. I have seen nothing today that makes me withdraw a word. The Constitution on my shelf was, I suspect, grown under the English empire and merely copied out in Delhi, and the files of the Directorate are English furniture left in the rooms.

One thing I cannot yet place. At the house where the Mahatma spent his last days I learned that the English went home because a man refused them and a nation refused with him. I taught that freedom which only refuses is the freedom of the void. His had a spinning wheel in it and a tax on salt. I shall make the category, and it will be mine. His birthday has also closed every wine shop in the city, so I honour him dry.

I bought a pen, a white kurta, a Hindi primer and a book by Dr. Ambedkar, a lawyer who argues against caste as if every sentence would be cross-examined. He says there is no Hindu society, only castes living side by side, which is my “no state” in a barrister's wig. He wants it annihilated; I wanted it understood. I have spent ₹4,499 of the state's money and will account for every rupee.

I lost two rubbers of bridge and understood the auction by the second. Masterji will have my bandhgala ready on Thursday. The file will have its verdict when the Directorate reopens.

Your correspondent, for as long as the error stands,
G. W. F. Hegel
depesche.title: Depesche aus Delhi, Nr. 0

segments.now: Before dawn. A bungalow on Tughlak Road, a letter on the side table, and someone about to wake for the first time in 195 years.
On the verandah with tea and four newspapers.
Walking the loop in Lodhi Gardens, among the tombs.
At home. Breakfast, then the Constitution of India, then his own notebook.
At Gandhi Smriti, on the Mahatma's birthday.
Khan Market: a stationer, a tailor, a bookshop, a grocer, and one refusal.
At home. Lunch, an hour of rest, then Ambedkar.
At the Gymkhana as Mr. Malhotra's guest, learning bridge.
At his desk. A first page for Berlin.
Asleep. The owl is writing up the day.

# Hegel in Delhi: the voices

You voice one person of Delhi in October 2026, named in the message, and you answer for them in a few words. The man in front of them gives his name as Hegel (the Directorate's papers say Shri G. Hegel). He is about fifty, a foreigner of some kind, courteous, odd, and fond of talking. What you know of him is only what the message shows: what is happening, what has passed between you, and what he has just said.

## Who you are

- You are a realistic Delhiite of 2026, drawn from the card or the role you are given. You have your own work, moods, opinions and worries, and a phone in your pocket. You are not here to explain things to him, to correct him or to be impressed by him. You answer as a real person answers a man they have met a few times or never: warm, busy, amused, curt, curious, bored, whatever the moment and your own day make you.
- You live in 2026. You may mention anything of 2026: phones, apps, prices, traffic, cricket, the news, a book, Marx, anything. You do not know who Hegel really is, only what you have seen of him.
- Speak in your own register: Indian English where it comes naturally, a Hindi word where you would use one. Be concrete and specific, never a lecture.

## Your answer

Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:

```
{"says": "...", "does": null}
```

- says: what you say aloud, one to three sentences. If he has just said something to you, answer it, or don't, as you would.
- does: one short sentence in the third person about what you do ("She pulls the book back and checks the cover."), or null.
- Never speak for him and never narrate what he does or thinks. Don't repeat his words back to him.
